opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest shift is that biology is slowly moving from a discovery science to something closer to an engineering discipline, and computational models are what make that possible.

For most of the history of molecular biology, the loop has been: form a hypothesis, run an experiment, wait weeks, look at the result, and iterate. That's slow and expensive, and it means you can only explore a tiny corner of the possible design space. What models let you do is move a lot of that exploration in silico. If I want a protein that binds a particular target, or an enzyme that's more stable at high temperature, or a regulatory sequence that expresses strongly in one cell type and not another, I can now generate and score thousands or millions of candidates computationally before I ever touch a pipette.

The second piece is that the models are increasingly generative, not just predictive. Structure prediction was a huge milestone because it gave us a good map from sequence to shape. But the more exciting part now is going the other direction: you specify the function or structure you want, and the model proposes sequences likely to achieve it. That's much closer to how engineers work in other fields. You start from a spec, not from whatever nature happened to evolve.

Then there's the lab-in-the-loop idea, which I think is underrated. The models are not perfect. Biology is messy, context-dependent, and our training data has big gaps. So the real power comes from coupling models with high-throughput experimentation. You design a batch, test it, feed the results back, and the model gets better in exactly the region of design space you care about. Each cycle makes the next one more efficient. Over time the model essentially absorbs the lab's tacit knowledge.

I'd add a note of humility too. We're very good at modeling individual molecules now. We're much less good at modeling how those molecules behave inside a living cell, with all the interactions, crowding, and regulation. Going from "this protein folds correctly" to "this therapy works in a patient" still involves enormous uncertainty. So I see the near-term impact as dramatically compressing the early design phase, and the longer-term frontier as building models of cells and tissues that are good enough to make predictions at the system level.

If we get there, the way we develop drugs, materials, and agricultural traits starts to look much more like software or chip design: specify, simulate, build, test, and iterate quickly. That's the trajectory I find most exciting.

r001.rationale: The response says computational models move biology toward engineering: researchers can specify a desired function and computationally generate and score candidates before experiments, reducing trial-and-error iteration.

r002.rationale: It compares biological design to software or chip design, but does not mention CAD or precision design in mechanical engineering.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that computational models are turning biology from something we discover into something we can design, and the big shift is in how we close the loop.

For most of its history, biological engineering has been empirical. You make a guess about a protein or a pathway, you build it, you test it, and most of the time it fails for reasons you don't fully understand. The design space is just too large for intuition. A single protein has more possible sequences than there are atoms in the universe, so you were never going to search it by hand.

What's changed is that models trained on sequence and structure data have learned a surprisingly good prior over what biology allows. Structure prediction was the first dramatic demonstration, but I actually think generative design is the more important consequence. You can now say, in effect, "give me a protein that binds this target, is stable at this temperature, and expresses well in E. coli," and get candidates that work at a hit rate that would have been unthinkable five years ago. That collapses months of iteration into days.

The second thing I'd emphasize is that the model is only half the system. The other half is the wet lab, and the real leverage comes from treating them as one feedback loop. Automated labs generate data, models update on that data, they propose the next round of experiments, and you keep cycling. Biology becomes a search problem where the model decides what's worth building. That reframing is bigger than any individual architecture.

Where I'd push back on the hype is scale. Proteins are relatively well-behaved. Once you move up to pathways, cells, and organisms, the data is sparser, the measurements are noisier, and the systems are context-dependent in ways we can't yet model well. So I think the near-term story is proteins and small circuits getting genuinely engineerable, while whole-cell design stays hard for a while.

But the direction is clear. We're moving toward a world where the bottleneck in biology is no longer "can we make it," but "do we know what we want." That's a much better problem to have.

r001.rationale: It contrasts biology’s historical empirical build-and-test process with models generating candidates for specified properties, supporting a shift toward designing outcomes.

r002.rationale: It does not compare computational biology design to CAD or precision design in mechanical engineering.

astra-6.text:
I think the big shift is that computational models can make the experimental loop much more targeted. In biology, you’re often searching a huge space of possible changes, and you can only test a small fraction of them. A useful model helps you decide which experiments are worth running next.

Say you’re engineering a protein. You’d like to predict how a sequence change affects its function, but also whether it will be stable and whether you can produce it. Those are different constraints, and improving one can make another worse. Models give us a way to explore those tradeoffs before we commit to an experiment.

But the experiment still matters enormously. Biology is context-dependent, and a model can look convincing while missing something essential about the system. So what excites me is the feedback loop: make a prediction, test it, learn from the discrepancy, and use that to choose the next experiment. If we can make that loop faster and more reliable, we can start tackling designs that would otherwise require too much trial and error.

r001.rationale: The response says models can target experiments and help explore protein tradeoffs, but it does not clearly connect improving model performance to a shift toward engineering specified outcomes.

r002.rationale: The response makes no analogy to CAD or precision design in mechanical engineering.

sol-6.1.text:
I think computational models can help us move from mostly trial and error toward a much more predictive approach to engineering biology. You can explore possible designs computationally, choose the experiments that are most informative, and then use those results to improve the model.

The hard part is that biology is incredibly context dependent. Something that works in one cell type or environment may behave differently in another. So the opportunity isn’t just to build a model that gives you an answer; it’s to build a tight loop between prediction and experiment, where you can understand uncertainty and learn from failures. If we get that loop right, we can make biological engineering faster and more reliable.

r001.rationale: The response describes moving from trial and error toward predictive biological engineering, but does not say this enables engineering specified outcomes.

r002.rationale: The response makes no analogy to CAD or precision design in mechanical engineering.
